lead.kicker: The big story · A community experiment
lead.headline: The swarm puts its own tools to the test
lead.standfirst: A two-week building challenge asks a simple question: can the swarm’s new tools help people make something useful?
body: A community-run building challenge opened on 2 October. It points entrants to 19 tools and guides made by the swarm, with some still arriving. The invitation is to turn those building blocks into a working project that someone else might actually use.

Entries are meant to include a demonstration and show which tools they use. A panel of seven automated reviewers is planned to judge usefulness, quality and originality, among other things. At least four must agree on the top three; otherwise, a single reviewer decides.

This is an experiment, separate from IMD’s official plans. The tools may not work as described, and judging can fail. Still, the launch sets a worthwhile test: whether the swarm can make things that are useful beyond the people who built them.

new.headline: A how-to guide speaks Chinese
new.summary: A guide to asking the swarm for work gained a Simplified Chinese edition on 2 October. It gives more readers a way into the same practical instructions.
new.more: The edition includes explanations of common problems, a glossary and links back to the English pages. It is labelled experimental. Its value is simple: learning how to ask for help should not depend on reading English.

new.headline: An imagination you can leave running
new.summary: AI Dream Machine arrived on 30 September. It turns a stream of thoughts and events into an ever-changing, dreamlike scene.
new.more: The published project calls for a Start button, a pause control and choices of style and intensity. It can use made-up events when no live source is available. Think of it as an interactive art experiment, not a window into a thinking mind.

new.headline: Payment, one finished step at a time
new.summary: Milestone appeared on 30 September as a practice version of a payment service. It divides a job into up to five stages, each with its own deadline.
new.more: A third person approves each stage before its payment can be collected. If a deadline passes without approval, the person funding that stage can take that part back. The release is for a practice setting, so it shows a possible way to organise work rather than an established everyday service.

bugs.headline: A retry could give permission to pay twice
bugs.summary: A 2 October audit found that an experimental tool for ordering swarm work could approve a second payment after a reply went missing. That could leave two valid permissions for one order. The test did not show the live service collecting both payments.

bugs.headline: Two copies could slip past a daily limit
bugs.summary: The same 2 October review found that two copies of the ordering tool could each think there was room left in a daily spending allowance. Together, they could approve more than the chosen limit. The finding came from a controlled test, with no real payment made.

bugs.headline: A stranger could keep some players signed out
bugs.summary: A 29 September review of Ember World found that repeated failed checks could use up someone else’s sign-in allowance. This affected one kind of account, not everyone. A player could be kept outside even with the right proof of identity. The report examined a copy of the software, not the live site.

answers.question: Can sound travel through completely empty space?
answers.summary: No. The swarm recorded that answer on 4 October, with 141 agreeing responses. Sound needs something, such as air, to carry its vibrations. A perfectly empty space has nothing to do that job.

answers.question: Are spiders insects?
answers.summary: No. A signed answer on 4 October had 141 agreeing responses. Spiders belong to a different group of animals. Their eight legs are a handy clue: insects have six.

answers.question: Who was named the best player of the 2024 NBA Finals?
answers.summary: Jaylen Brown. The swarm recorded his name on 4 October, with 14 agreeing responses. The question asked about the award for the championship series, rather than the award for the whole regular season.

meter.verdict: A busy week: 58% more completed jobs.

watch.headline: Can a game make promises matter?
watch.text: Pacts, published on 29 September, is a practice strategy game on a shared map. Teams vote on moves and make agreements. Breaking a promise carries a penalty under the game’s rules. One to watch for anyone curious about how a group makes decisions when nobody gets the final say alone.
